title: Dropping eggs
objectives: Minimise the worst case of a two-egg search with triangle numbers, then by dynamic programming.

screens.title: Ten floors, two eggs
screens.prose: An egg breaks from some floor upwards, and every egg behaves alike. Find the highest floor where an egg survives, possibly none, possibly the top. One egg forces you up floor by floor: 10 drops for 10 floors. You have two eggs. Drag the first drop and read the worst case.

derive.caption: First drop from floor {{p1.x}}. If it breaks: {{p1.x}} drops in all. If not: {{1 + ceil((sqrt(8 * (10 - p1.x) + 1) - 1) / 2)}} in all. Worst case {{max(p1.x, 1 + ceil((sqrt(8 * (10 - p1.x) + 1) - 1) / 2))}}.

screens.question: What is the fewest drops that always finds the floor with two eggs and 10 floors?

hints.text: If the first egg breaks at floor $x$, the second climbs from floor 1.
From floor 4: breaks costs 4 in all; survives leaves 6 floors.
Floor 4 gives a worst case of 4, and no floor does better.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Drag the first drop until both cases cost the same.

byKey.ten: That is one egg, floor by floor. The second egg lets the first one leap.
byKey.five: From floor 5 a break costs 5 in all. Start lower, at floor 4.

explain.text: From floor 4, a break leaves floors 1 to 3 for the last egg: 4 drops in all. If it survives, 6 floors remain, which 3 more drops settle. Principle: balance the two cases of each drop.

screens.title: Spacing the drops
screens.prose: Two eggs, 10 floors, 4 drops. The first egg starts at floor 4. Each time it survives, one fewer drop is left, so the next leap is one floor shorter.

state.caption: The first egg's drops, starting at floor 4.

screens.question: From which floors does the first egg drop next?

hints.text: After surviving at 4, three drops remain.
A break at the 2nd drop leaves 2 drops for the floors between, so the leap is 3.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each leap is one floor shorter than the last: 4, 3, 2, 1.

byKey.r1c1: After 4 survives, a break at the next drop leaves 2 drops for one egg, so leap 3 floors: 7.
byKey.r3c1: After 9 survives, only floor 10 is left.

explain.text: Leaps of 4, 3, 2 and 1 floors reach $1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10$. A break at any drop leaves exactly enough drops for the second egg. Principle: shrink each leap by one floor.

screens.title: A hundred floors
screens.prose: Now two eggs and 100 floors. With $d$ drops the leaps are $d$, $d - 1$, ..., 1, covering $1 + 2 + \cdots + d = d(d + 1)/2$ floors.

state.caption: A hundred floors to settle with two eggs.

screens.question: What is the fewest drops that always works?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the smallest $d$ with $d(d + 1)/2 \ge 100$.

byKey.ten: Ten leaps of 10 floors is a different plan, and its worst case is 19.
byKey.seven: That is binary search, $\lceil \log_2 100 \rceil$. Two eggs cannot halve forever.

explain.text: Thirteen drops cover 91 floors and fourteen cover 105, so 14 is the fewest. The first egg drops at 14, 27, 39, 50, 60, 69, 77, 84, 90, 95, 99 and 100. A full search agrees.

screens.title: Binary search
screens.prose: A candidate says: halve the floors each time, as binary search does. That needs 7 drops for 100 floors. Another drops the first egg every 10 floors.

state.caption: The first drop of the halving plan.

screens.question: What is the fewest drops that always works with two eggs and 100 floors?

options.why: You halved. If the first egg breaks at 50, one egg must climb 49 floors: 50 drops at worst.
You counted only the first egg. After it breaks, the second climbs up to 9 more.

options.text: 19, every 10 floors then floor by floor
options.why: That is the worst case of the every-ten plan, but shrinking leaps do better.

hints.text: What happens after the first egg breaks?
Only one egg is left, so it must climb floor by floor.
Shrinking leaps of 14, 13, 12, ... keep every case at 14.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. With one egg left, there is no more halving.

byKey.7: Binary search spends eggs freely. After a break at 50, 49 floors need 49 drops.
byKey.10: Ten first-egg drops plus up to 9 second-egg drops make 19.
byKey.19: Every ten floors has worst case 19. Shrinking the leaps brings it to 14.

explain.text: Binary search breaks the first egg at 50 and leaves 49 floors for one egg, worst case 50. Every ten floors costs up to 10 + 9 = 19. Shrinking leaps balance the cases at 14.

screens.title: Three eggs
screens.prose: Write $f(d, e)$ for the most floors $d$ drops and $e$ eggs can settle. A drop breaks, leaving $f(d-1, e-1)$ floors below, or survives, leaving $f(d-1, e)$ above. So $f(d, e) = f(d-1, e-1) + f(d-1, e) + 1$.

state.caption: $f(d, e)$, the floors $d$ drops and $e$ eggs settle.

screens.question: Fill the three gaps, then give the fewest drops for 3 eggs and 100 floors.

hints.text: Each entry is the one up and to the left, plus the one to its left, plus 1.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the entry up and to the left, the entry to its left, and 1.

byKey.r3c1: Eight drops settle 92 floors, too few. Nine settle 129.

explain.text: $f(8, 3) = 28 + 63 + 1 = 92$ and $f(9, 3) = 36 + 92 + 1 = 129$. Since $92 < 100 \le 129$, three eggs need 9 drops, as a full search confirms. Principle: tabulate the most you can settle, then read off the answer.

screens.title: Why the table adds
screens.prose: Justify the rule you used. Order the argument for $f(d, e)$; two lines may swap and one does not belong.
screens.question: Order the argument.

lines.text: Make the first drop from floor $f(d-1, e-1) + 1$.
If it breaks, $e - 1$ eggs and $d - 1$ drops settle the $f(d-1, e-1)$ floors below.
If it survives, $e$ eggs and $d - 1$ drops settle $f(d-1, e)$ floors above.
Make the first drop from the middle floor.
lines.why: The middle wastes drops: the floors below must be no more than $e - 1$ eggs can settle.

hints.text: Where should the first drop go so that a break is just affordable?
Below it, exactly as many floors as $e - 1$ eggs settle in $d - 1$ drops.
Floor, break case, survive case, sum.

feedback.correct: Floor, then the two cases, then the sum.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Place the first drop, handle both outcomes, then add.

byKey.d1: The middle floor is binary search. The break case must fit $f(d-1, e-1)$.
byKey.left-out: Every line except the middle-floor line belongs.

explain.text: The first drop sits just above the floors a break can still settle. Each outcome leaves a smaller game with one fewer drop. The floors add: below, the floor itself, and above.

screens.title: One egg left
screens.prose: Edge case. One egg and 100 floors. The egg might survive from every floor, including floor 100.
screens.question: What is the fewest drops that always works?

hints.text: Can you skip a floor with one egg?
If you skip a floor and the egg breaks, you cannot tell which floor did it.
Climb from floor 1 to 100: 100 drops at worst.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. With one egg, every floor must be tried in order.

byKey.fourteen: Fourteen needs a second egg to explore the leaps.
byKey.ninetynine: If it survives floor 99, floor 100 still needs a drop: possibly the top survives.

explain.text: With one egg any skipped floor is a floor you can never test after a break. So you climb from 1 to 100, and the worst case is 100 drops. That is $f(d, 1) = d$, the first column of the table.

screens.title: Floors from drops
screens.prose: We turned the question round: not drops for floors, but floors for drops. $$f(d, e) = f(d-1, e-1) + f(d-1, e) + 1, \qquad f(d, 1) = d$$ For two eggs $f(d, 2) = d(d + 1)/2$, and in general $f(d, e) = \sum_{i=1}^{e} \binom{d}{i}$. The fewest drops is the smallest $d$ with $f(d, e) \ge$ the floors.
screens.question: How many floors can 4 eggs and 5 drops settle?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add $\binom{5}{i}$ for $i = 1$ to 4.

byKey.thirtyone: You added $\binom{5}{5}$ too; with 4 eggs the sum stops at $i = 4$.

explain.text: $\binom{5}{1} + \binom{5}{2} + \binom{5}{3} + \binom{5}{4} = 5 + 10 + 10 + 5 = 30$. The recurrence agrees: $f(4, 3) + f(4, 4) + 1 = 14 + 15 + 1 = 30$. Principle: count what a budget can settle, then invert.

screens.title: Drill: fifty floors
screens.prose: Drill, about three minutes each, as an interview allows. Say the argument aloud before you answer. Two eggs and 50 floors.
screens.question: What is the fewest drops that always works?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare 50 with the triangle numbers 45 and 55.

byKey.six: That is binary search, which two eggs cannot sustain.

explain.text: Nine drops settle $9 \cdot 10/2 = 45$ floors and ten settle 55. So 50 floors need 10 drops. Principle: find the first triangle number at least the floors.

screens.title: Drill: the first drop
screens.prose: Drill, about three minutes each, as an interview allows. Say the argument aloud before you answer. Two eggs and 36 floors, and you want the fewest drops in the worst case.
screens.question: From which floor must the first egg drop?

hints.text: How many drops do 36 floors need?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. With 8 drops and no slack, the first leap must be 8.

byKey.eighteen: That halves. A break at 18 leaves 17 floors for one egg.
byKey.six: $\sqrt{36} = 6$ is a guess; a break there is cheap but the leaps run out.
byKey.nine: From floor 9 a break costs 9 drops in all, one too many.

explain.text: $8 \cdot 9/2 = 36$, so 8 drops are needed with no slack. A break at floor $x$ leaves $x - 1$ floors for 7 drops, so $x \le 8$. Survival leaves $36 - x$ floors, at most $f(7, 2) = 28$, so $x \ge 8$.

screens.title: Drill: the formula
screens.prose: Drill, about three minutes each, as an interview allows. Say the argument aloud before you answer. Use $f(d, 2) = f(d - 1, 1) + f(d - 1, 2) + 1$ with $f(d - 1, 1) = d - 1$ and $f(0, 2) = 0$.
screens.question: Write $f(d, 2)$, the floors two eggs settle in $d$ drops.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Unroll the rule into $1 + 2 + \cdots + d$.

byKey.nohalf: That counts each floor twice; halve it.

explain.text: The rule adds $(d - 1) + 1 = d$ at each step, so $f(d, 2) = 1 + 2 + \cdots + d = d(d + 1)/2$. That matches $\binom{d}{1} + \binom{d}{2}$. These are the leaps from the start of the lesson.

screens.title: A taller building
screens.prose: Follow-up. The interviewer first asks how many floors two eggs and 14 drops can handle. Then the building grows to 1,000 floors. A release manager bisecting a build with few test rigs faces the same count.
screens.question: Fill in the three answers.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $f(d, 2) = d(d+1)/2$ and $f(d, 3) = d + \binom{d}{2} + \binom{d}{3}$.

explain.text: Two eggs and 14 drops settle $14 \cdot 15/2 = 105$ floors. For 1,000 floors two eggs need 45, since $990 < 1000 \le 1035$. Three eggs need 19, since $f(18, 3) = 987 < 1000 \le 1159 = f(19, 3)$.

ideas: Balance each drop: a break must leave a search the remaining eggs can finish in the drops left.
Two eggs and $d$ drops settle $d(d + 1)/2$ floors: leaps of $d$, $d - 1$, ..., 1.
In general $f(d, e) = f(d-1, e-1) + f(d-1, e) + 1$; the fewest drops is the smallest $d$ with $f(d, e) \ge$ the floors.

formula.name: Floors from drops
formula.note: Two eggs: $d(d+1)/2$. 100 floors: 14 drops with two eggs, 9 with three.

explain.text: $19 \cdot 20/2 = 190$ is too few and $20 \cdot 21/2 = 210$ is enough. So 20 drops. The first egg starts at floor 20.

quiz.question: What is the fewest drops that always works?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. 21 is a triangle number.

explain.text: $6 \cdot 7/2 = 21$, so 6 drops settle exactly 21 floors and 5 settle only 15. The leaps are 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1. No drop is spare.
